newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK post-handover government brushes off Blair snub.
newsitem.headline: HK post-handover government brushes off Blair snub.

text.p: Hong Kong's future government on Thursday shrugged off a snub by British Prime Minister Tony Blair who has decided to boycott a ceremony to inaugurate the controversial post-handover legislature.

The swearing-in will be "a ceremony which will show that the executive branch, legislature and the judiciary are all taking office at the same time", said Rita Fan, president of the provisional legislature, which Britain has sharply denounced.
The plan to install the legislature promptly after the flag change, while international VIPs who come for the handover party are still in town, would not be changed, Fan said.

The United States earlier announced it too would shun the inauguration, reflecting Western disapproval that the unelected chamber replaces a democratically-elected parliament from July 1 when China takes over Hong Kong after 156 years of colonialism.
The timing of the swearing-in was decided by a China-controlled committee.

"The Preparatory Committee decided about half a month ago that the swearing-in ceremony of taking office is a group thing," Fan said. Future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa, senior government officials and top judges will also be sworn in during the ceremony, in the first hour or so of July 1.

More than 4,000 guests invited by Britain and China are expected to witness a glitzy joint handover ceremony on the night of June 30, marking the end of Britain's once-sprawling empire in Asia and China's national shame.

Blair and VIPs from other countries that contest the legitimacy of the provisional legislature were put in a diplomatic bind by China's plans to swear in the unelected chamber at the same venue immediately after the handover.
Blair said on Wednesday he would attend the handover ceremony, but officials made clear he would leave before the provisional legislature is sworn in.
Heir to the throne Prince Charles and Foreign Secretary Robin Cook will also attend as Britain's top representatives.
Colonial Governor Chris Patten welcomed Blair's plan to attend but said he hoped China would back down on its plan to swear in the provisional legislature just after the handover.
But Patten said he had not urged any foreign leaders to boycott China's ceremony.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who will lead a the U.S. delegation, said on Tuesday she would turn down an invitation to the swearing-in ceremony.
Political analyst Michael DeGolyer said discord between Beijing and London over Patten's democratic reforms had set the stage for the "awkward dispute" surrounding the ceremonies.

"It's been very clear that we were going to have some rather awkward moments to say the least ever since the breakdown of the negotiations back with the dispute over the Patten reforms," DeGolyer, director of a long-term study on the transition based at Hong Kong's Baptist University, said.
DeGolyer said the handover would be a matter of "you have your party and I'll have mine", with any interaction between the British and Chinese kept as formal and ceremonial as possible.
China ended months of speculation on Wednesday by announcing President Jiang Zemin would lead its delegation, the first visit to the territory by a Chinese head of state.
But Jiang's visit will be fleeting.

He will receive the territory of 6.4 million people from Prince Charles, then remain just long enough for the swearing-in of the new administration before flying home for China's own mammoth celebration on the streets of Beijing.

Premier Li Peng, scorned by many Hong Kong people as a "butcher of Beijing" for his perceived role in unleashing the 1989 miltary crackdown in China, and Vice-Premier Qian Qichen, as well as other top officials will accompany Jiang on the trip.
